title: Spiral galaxy NGC 55
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 55, imaged by the 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Red patches of nebulosity mark regions of active star formation in NGC 55, a nearby galaxy in this image from a 0.9-meter National Science Foundation telescope at Chile's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.
NGC 55 lies about five million light-years away and belongs to the Sculptor Group, a small gathering of galaxies.

The red glow in regions like these comes from hydrogen gas energized by hot, young stars that have recently formed inside the clouds, so each red patch is a sign of stellar birth. A galaxy group such as the Sculptor Group is a small collection of galaxies bound loosely together by gravity. Our own Milky Way belongs to a similar gathering, the Local Group. Relatively nearby galaxies like NGC 55 are close enough that astronomers can study their star-forming regions in some detail, comparing them with those in our own Galaxy. NGC 55 lies in the constellation Sculptor.
scale: NGC 55 is about five million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo observed NGC 55 in visible light through B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, making star-forming regions much more prominent than they would be to the eye.
